newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Central Africa needs mini Marshall Plan.
newsitem.headline: Central Africa needs mini Marshall Plan.

text.p: Mohamed Sahnoun, the new U.N. envoy for Central Africa, said on Tuesday a "mini Marshall Plan" was needed if the region was ever to recover from the scars of warfare and genocide.

"Some of the scars are impossible to heal in the short term," Sahnoun said at his first news conference since he was appointed by Secretary-General Kofi Annan last week, adding that the prospects for an immediate peace "were slim."

He said there were bound to be "tragic consequences" if Zaire, Burundi and Rwanda were not helped by "some kind of a mini Marshall Plan," a reference to massive U.S. aid to help put a devastated Europe on its feet in 1948 after the Second World War.

"We have to let them know that if they create the political conditions the international community will be fothcoming to help them resolve the deep economic, social and environmental problems. This is one of the most precarious, most sensitive regions of the world," he said.

Sahnoun, a veteran Algerian diplomat, assigned to what some call a "mission impossible" to solve the crises in Central Africa, briefed the Security Council but revealed few details on his plans, saying he needed to speak to all official and unofficial political leaders first.

Council diplomats said the response to Sahnoun's economic assistance proposal was positive but no figures were discussed. "There needs to be some incentive, a reward for a peace agreement," said one senior envoy.
Sahnoun said he would meet Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko next week week in Nice, France, where he is recovering from cancer surgery, before going to the region. He will be based in Nairobi.

His assignment focuses on a civil war led by ethnic Tutsis in eastern Zaire, ethnic war in Burundi and collective trauma in Rwanda after the 1994 genocide by Hutus of up to 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus. These conflicts have spawned millions of refugees and displaced people, a mini arms race and deep hostilities between regional leaders.

Asked repeatedly about Zaire's planned offensive against Rwanda-backed rebels in the east, Sahnoun said he understood why Zaire saw its sovereignty threatened but that "every effort should be made to convince Zaire that they should give a chance to a ... peaceful solution."
The rebels have seized territory bordering Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi. Mobutu has vowed the army will crush them.
He was also asked if the fighting was a proxy war for big powers, with France supporting Zaire and the United States favouring Rwanda.
"I would like to believe it is a problem of bad governance, degredation of the environment," he replied. "Foreign interference exists in one way or another but it is a fallout."
Sahnoun is the first special representative of both the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
His last assignment with the United Nations was in 1992 when he clashed with Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali and resigned as special representative in Somalia after six months on the job.

He felt obliged to resign after Boutros-Ghali rebuked him for saying the United Nations was slow in reacting to famine in the Horn of Africa country. Asked about the clash on Tuesday, he said: "I think he did his duty. I did mine. This happens in the world. It is human nature."
